{"content": "# Daily and Hourly Scrutiny

## The image

Of all the sentences Darwin wrote about natural selection, this is the one most often quoted:

> "It may be said that natural selection is daily and hourly scrutinising, throughout the world, every variation, even the slightest; rejecting that which is bad, preserving and adding up all that is good; silently and insensibly working, whenever and wherever opportunity offers, at the improvement of each organic being in relation to its organic and inorganic conditions of life."

Unpack it slowly, because every clause is doing work.

- **Daily and hourly, throughout the world.** The process is not an occasional event, a catastrophe, or a special intervention. It is continuous and universal.
- **Every variation, even the slightest.** Nothing is too small to be examined. This is the claim the rest of the chapter has to defend, and Darwin defends it with examples of characters we would dismiss as trivial.
- **Rejecting the bad, preserving and adding up the good.** Two operations, not one. Rejection removes; *adding up* accumulates. A single preserved variation is nothing; the summation over generations is everything.
- **Silently and insensibly.** Nothing visible happens. There is no moment you could photograph.
- **In relation to its organic and inorganic conditions of life.** "Improvement" is never improvement in the abstract. It is always improvement *relative to* the climate, the soil, the competitors, the predators, the prey. Change the conditions and yesterday's improvement is today's handicap.

## Why we see nothing

Darwin immediately draws the consequence: "We see nothing of these slow changes in progress, until the hand of time has marked the long lapse of ages." And even then our sight is poor. The geological record is so imperfect that when we finally do look back, "we only see that the forms of life are now different from what they formerly were."

Notice how modest this is. The fossil record does not hand us the process; it hands us a before-and-after comparison with the middle missing. Darwin is admitting, at the very moment of stating his theory most grandly, that the direct evidence for it is a difference between two snapshots.

## Trifling characters are not trifling

Natural selection can act only through and for the good of each being. But Darwin's point is that "good" reaches into characters we would have called negligible.

**Colour in insects and birds.** Leaf-eating insects are green; bark-feeders are mottled-grey. The alpine ptarmigan is white in winter, the red-grouse is the colour of heather, the black-grouse the colour of peaty earth. Darwin's inference is that these tints preserve their owners from danger. His supporting argument is a chain:

1. Grouse, if not destroyed at some period of their lives, would increase in countless numbers — so something is killing most of them.
2. They are known to suffer largely from birds of prey.
3. Hawks are guided *by eyesight* to their prey.

Step 3 is the crucial link, and Darwin backs it with a homely fact: on parts of the Continent people are warned not to keep white pigeons, because they are the most liable to destruction. Given all three steps, he can see no reason to doubt that natural selection gives each kind of grouse its proper colour — and, once acquired, keeps that colour true and constant. Selection is a preserver as well as a maker.

**The white sheep.** Someone might object that killing off the occasional oddly-coloured animal could hardly matter much. Darwin answers with a breeder's practice: in a flock of white sheep it is *essential* to destroy every lamb with the faintest trace of black. Breeders know that steady removal of the faintly deviant is what holds a character constant. Nature does the same thing without intending it.

**Fruit.** Botanists consider the down on a fruit and the colour of its flesh characters of the most trifling importance. Yet the horticulturist Downing reports from the United States that:

| Character | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Smooth skin vs. down | Smooth-skinned fruits suffer far more from a beetle, a curculio |
| Purple vs. yellow plums | Purple plums suffer far more from a certain disease |
| Yellow flesh in peaches | A different disease attacks yellow-fleshed peaches far more than other-coloured flesh |

The argument Darwin extracts is an *a fortiori* one: if these slight differences make a great difference even in an orchard, *with all the aids of art* — with a gardener spraying, pruning, and protecting — then in a state of nature, where trees must struggle with other trees and with a host of enemies, such differences would effectually settle which variety succeeds. The cultivated case is the weak case, and it already shows the effect.

## What to carry away

The rhetorical structure of this passage is worth noticing. Darwin makes an enormous claim (constant worldwide scrutiny of the slightest variation), then concedes that we cannot watch it happen, then rescues the claim by showing that even characters chosen for their apparent insignificance — down on a plum, a trace of black in a lamb — turn out to have life-and-death consequences once you look.
